items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.title: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now les
items.summary:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

Relative to the number of researchers in each field, Claude is used more in the formal sciences, such as computer science, mathematics, and statistics, and less in health and lab-based physical sciences. Scientists primarily use Claude to analyze data and to write. Data analysis alone accounts for about one-third of sessions on Claude and nearly half of sessions on Claude Code. Scientists use it less for idea generation and data gathering, even though, in an [...] Claude use is also disproportionately high in predominantly cognitive tasks. By contrast, Claude use is low for physical and interpersonal tasks. Claude use is also lower for tasks where regulatory barriers limit AI assistance. Overall, across the spectrum of highly specialized research tasks, usage and capability measures are strongly related. [...] Claude use across scientific fields. Each dot represents a field. The horizontal axis shows the field’s share of researchers, and the vertical axis shows the field’s share of research sessions, both on log scales. items.title: Claude Code settings files expose thousands of secrets on GitHub - Ars Technica
items.summary: The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local “.claude/settings.local.json” file on the user’s computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it. [...] Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.

items.title: State of the Climate Update for COP31
items.summary:
Full Report Press Release Data Hub

The WMO State of the Climate Update 2026 shows that the past 12 years (2015–2026) are set to be the warmest on record. The global average surface temperature from January to September was about 1.47 °C above the 1850–1900 pre-industrial average. El Niño has intensified since August and is expected to reach record strength by December. [...] El Niño releases heat from the ocean and is expected to increase the risk of extreme heat, drought and heavy rainfall well into 2027. Global mean sea level reached its highest point in the satellite record, which began in 1993. Preliminary data through July point to a tenth consecutive year of record ocean heat content. [...] The WMO State of the Climate 2026 Update was released on the first day of the UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Türkiye, as an authoritative, science-based report. It includes data – where available – up to September 2026 and therefore does not reflect the most recent impacts of El Niño.

items.title: State of the climate: 2026 likely to tie with 2024 as the warmest year on record
items.summary:
Western Europe and the Mediterranean were also unusually warm, with temperatures around 3C above average over France and the western Mediterranean Sea. North-west Russia, the Canadian Arctic, south-central North America, eastern Africa and parts of west Antarctica were also exceptionally warm.

The most notable part of the planet that was colder than usual was the Weddell Sea sector of Antarctica, which came in at more than 2C below average for the season. [...] The best estimate for 2026 is now around 1.52C above pre-industrial levels, with a 90% range of 1.50C to 1.55C. This is slightly higher – but effectively tied with – the prior record of 1.52C set in 2024.

It marks a slight increase from Carbon Brief’s previous projection of 1.51C, set out in its July’s “state of the climate” update.

There is an approximately 67% chance of setting a new record this year in the average of the six-datasets examined. [...] The rise in global temperatures is a symptom of Earth’s rising energy imbalance. This is the difference between the energy the planet absorbs from the sun and the energy it radiates back to space.

As long as this energy imbalance is positive, the Earth system accumulates heat, around 90% of which ends up in the oceans.

items.title: Six climate and health actions could save 1.6 million lives and deliver trillions in benefits each year
items.summary: “The climate crisis is a health crisis, but much of the harm it causes can be prevented with tools we already have,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “This report shows that scaling up proven, affordable actions could save millions of lives, with the greatest gains in the countries that need them most. As governments prepare for the next round of climate negotiations, protecting health must be at the centre of climate action.” [...] Released ahead of COP31, where governments are expected to share their climate commitments, the report underscores that many health impacts of climate change are preventable with solutions available today. But these solutions must be implemented across health and health-determining sectors to help anticipate, prevent, prepare for and reduce climate-related health risks. [...] The report, Global benefits and costs of prioritized actions on climate change and health, is the first comprehensive analysis of the economic and fiscal returns from taking six WHO-recommended actions to scale. Together, the findings point to a triple dividend from these climate actions: healthier people, lower emissions, and stronger economies.

a robot expo. a crowd of phones. 
a girl with a glowing metal core where her waist should be. ✨
someone holds a little fan to it. she smiles, fixes her hair. 

the face? almost certainly AI. 
the fan? that's real robotics. 🔥
every motor, every battery, every AI chip makes heat. 🌡️
heat is one of the reasons real humanoids still work in short shifts and spend hours on chargers. 

so how far have robots actually come? 👇

📅 2015: at the DARPA challenge, robots fell over opening doors.
🤸 2025: humanoids do flips, box, and dance at expos.
📦 2025: Unitree shipped 5,500+ humanoids. AgiBot's CEO said 5,000+.
🇺🇸 Tesla, Figure and Agility: about 150 each (Omdia).
🏭 Hyundai plans a factory for 30,000 robots a year by 2028.

💰 Morgan Stanley: a $5 trillion humanoid market by 2050.
ten years from falling over to doing backflips. 
but the robots that exist are still grey, bulky and plugged in. 🔌

the "robot girl" is what the hype looks like.
the fan is what the engineering looks like. 🛠️
when the real ones catch up with this video, will you be able to tell the difference? 👀

items.title: SHE LOOKS HUMAN. EVEN HER REACTIONS ARE STARTING TO FEEL REAL.
items.summary:
SHE LOOKS HUMAN. EVEN HER REACTIONS ARE STARTING TO FEEL REAL.

At a tech expo, a young woman approaches a humanoid robot and says, “I love your hair.”

The robot smiles, touches its hair, and responds to her.

People nearby stop to watch. Some pull out their phones. Others step closer to see how it reacts.

But look beneath its face.

Exposed wires, motors, and glowing electronic components reveal the machinery behind the human appearance.

The interesting part is how quickly humanoid robots are moving beyond basic movement and industrial tasks. They're now being designed to look human, express emotions, and interact naturally with people.

The technology still has a long way to go. But once robots combine realistic faces, natural movement, and convincing conversation, the potential market could be much bigger than people expect.

Some companies may end up selling more than robots.

They may be selling the feeling of interacting with another human.

items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

CAPEWEEK: The Great American Aerospace and Technology Expo is America's national annual gathering for aerospace and the technologies converging with it, including defense, superintelligence, energy, autonomy, robotics and advanced mobility on land, sea, air and space. Held on the 15,000-foot former space shuttle landing runway at NASA's Kennedy Space Center, CAPEWEEK combines a leadership forum, an international industry exposition and public days featuring a world-class air show and technology [...] CAPEWEEK will convene companies working across aerospace, defense, superintelligence, energy, autonomy, robotics and advanced mobility on land, sea, air and space, from rockets and fighter jets to autonomous ships, electric vehicles and delivery drones. Its leadership forum will bring executives, investors and government officials together to collaborate across these sectors. [...] Go Back

KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Fla. (Nov. 5, 2026) - CAPEWEEK, a new annual aerospace and technology expo announced today, will debut March 27 through April 2, 2028, on the 15,001-foot former space shuttle landing runway at NASA's Kennedy Space Center. The event will combine a leadership forum, an industry exposition and public days featuring flight demonstrations and technology displays. CAPEWEEK is designed to grow to accommodate more than 500,000 people a year.
